new_statements.quote: Arbore has all the features typical of the phonologies of East Cushitic languages. The characteristic three-term stop series is strongly in evidence. There is the usual system of five vowels. There are the customary rigid constraints on segmental distribution, which provide one source for the fairly elaborate sets of morpheme alternations found throughout the group. Both consonantal and vocalic length are phonologically significant. There is also the expected two-term accentual system, one characteristic of which is that it has a greater degree of significance in grammar than in lexis.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (13 pp., Rosetta Project scan of Hayward 1984, Chapter Two "Phonology"). The quoted passage is on pdf page 1 exactly as reported, both in the text layer (extracted text and the) and on the rendered page image: "Arbore has all the features typical of the phonologies of East Cushitic languages.... There is also the expected two-term accentual system, one characteristic of which is that it has a greater degree of significance in grammar than in lexis." Locator check: pdf p.1 is the chapter-opening page and carries no printed folio; pdf p.3 shows folio 51 at the page top, so p.1 = printed p.49 as the reader says. The excerpt runs from the chapter introduction through 2.1 (segments)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Arbore has a two-term (accented vs. unaccented) accentual system of the East Cushitic tonal-accent type; the accent is primarily grammatical (morphosyntactically determined) rather than lexically contrastive. The source excerpt does not state the position of the accent in the word; the placement rule is in the unexcerpted accent section of Hayward 1984.
new_statements.domain_note: General characterization of the word-level accentual system in the chapter introduction; Hayward's transcription marks accent with acute on vowels (e.g. gaabbá 'younger sibling', hakkó 'egg', kollá 'leaf, wing' on pp. 51, 57). The section that states where the accent falls and its grammatical functions comes later in Chapter Two and is not in the open excerpt.
new_statements.identity_note: Hayward 1984 describes the Arbore spoken at Gondorobba (Ethiopian administrative name Irbore) by informants of the Marle and Gondorobba divisions (last informant 1982); no dialect split is given a separate glottocode. Glottolog alternative names: Arbora, Arborie, Erbore, Irbore; ethnonym also Hor. WALS code 'abo'.
